item.title: The Night Watch
item.lesson: Amsterdam's civic militia companies commissioned group portraits the way corporations commission lobby art, and the formula was fixed: rows of dignified faces, each member paying for his spot. Rembrandt blew the formula apart. His militiamen under Captain Frans Banninck Cocq are caught mid-motion — mustering, loading, drumming, a dog barking, a mysterious girl in gold (the company's mascot, with a dead chicken at her belt, its claws a pun on their name, the Kloveniers) glowing in the crowd. It is a portrait pretending to be a history painting, and it made standing still look obsolete. Two corrections to the legend: it is not a night scene — darkened varnish earned it the nickname a century later — and it was never rejected; it hung with honor, though it was brutally trimmed on all four sides in 1715 to fit a wall in the Town Hall. The missing strip of composition is known today only from an old copy.
item.lookFor: Behind the militiaman in the dark red sash, half-hidden at the back, a single eye peeks over shoulders beneath a beret — widely believed to be Rembrandt himself, watching his own revolution.
